entities.summary: Ertuğrul or Ertuğrul Ghazi was a 13th-century uch bey (marcher-lord), who was the father of Osman I. Little is known about Ertuğrul's life. According to Ottoman tradition, he was the son of Suleyman Shah, the leader of the Kayı tribe of the Oghuz Turks, which fled from western Central Asia to Anatolia to escape the Mongol conquests; but according to contemporary numinastic evidence, he was the son of Gündüz Alp. According to the legend, after the death of his father, Ertuğrul and his followers entered the service of the Sultanate of Rum, for which he was rewarded with dominion over the town of Söğüt on the frontier with the Byzantine Empire.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ertuğrul's leadership and strategic alliances played a crucial role in establishing the Ottoman Empire, which would eventually become one of the most influential empires in world history. His legacy as the father of Osman I paved the way for the Ottoman conquests that shaped the Middle East and Eastern Europe.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ertuğrul's leadership and military prowess laid the foundation for the Ottoman Empire, which would go on to shape regional politics and culture in the Middle East and beyond. His legacy as a national hero continues to influence Turkish identity.
